extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, equity practitioners, and legal scholars (attorneys/judges handling patent infringement suits)
extracted.subtask_short: equity pleading and trial in patent suits
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing pleadings (answers, cross-bills, supplemental bills, amendments) and modes of trial (feigned issues, jury, depositions) in equity patent infringement litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer under oath — compliance and corporate limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an answer under oath is demanded the demand must be complied with, if the defendant has the capacity to take an oath. A bill against a corporation cannot contain this demand unless its officers are made parties, — the corporate body being unable to comply, although a corporation may be called upon to answer interrogatories and must give such replies as the knowledge of its officers permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a plaintiff demands an oath, defendants capable of oath must comply. For corporations, the officers should be made parties to compel an oath; otherwise compel answers via interrogatories and answers reflecting officers' knowledge. (Colgate v. Compagnie Francaise and related authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight required to overthrow a sworn answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant's answer, if responsive to the allegations of the bill, must be overthrown by the evidence of two witnesses, or of one witness and circumstances equivalent to another, or, at least, sufficient to make a preponderance of testimony in favor of complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sworn answer standing as testimony is not lightly displaced — plaintiff needs typically two witnesses or equivalent corroboration (or preponderance) to overthrow it. This is why complainants sometimes insist on answers under oath rather than waive them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and evidentiary advantage of oral examination vs. sworn answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicitors ... seem to overlook the great disadvantages under which they often labor in not waiving an answer under oath in equity cases, now that the complainant and defendant are themselves both competent witnesses, and can be orally examined under Equity Rule 67.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consideration: allowing oral testimony may provide fresher evidence and opportunity for direct examination/cross-examination; waiving sworn answer may be strategic disadvantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for pleading special defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer, containing a statement of any defence of which special notice is required in actions at law, must be filed a sufficient time before the trial, or the plaintiff may insist on a continuance. That a plea or notice at law setting up special defences under the statute must be served or filed at least thirty days before the term of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special defenses must be timely — statutes/rules (e.g., 30 days before trial) govern; failure may entitle plaintiff to continuance. Equity follows substantially the same practice as law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate and joint answers; oath and amendment of joint answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the defendants may answer separately from the others, or where it can be done without confusion all may join. A joint answer cannot be sworn to by a part of the defendants, though such an answer may be amended by erasing the non-juring parties and be allowed to stand as the reply of those who have made oath to its averments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants can plead separately; a partially sworn joint answer must be cured by removing non‑sworn parties if necessary. A defendant who neither joined nor filed a separate answer cannot appear and answer after a final decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to answers for defects of form or scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to an answer on account of defects of form, or the omission of necessary allegations, or the insertion of scandalous and impertinent matter, must be taken by exceptions, and if these are sustained the answer must be amended by such alterations, expurgations, or additions as it may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exceptions to challenge pleadings; court will order appropriate amendment/expurgation if exception sustained. Equity Rules referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: General replication effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of the answer, and its amendment if excepted to, is followed by the general replication, which puts the cause at issue without rejoinder or further pleadings upon either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the answer (and any amendments) is in and replication filed, the pleadings are at issue — no further pleadings except by leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-bill — permissible scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant, in an action in equity, is entitled to relief against the plaintiff, in some matter connected with the suit, he may file a cross-bill with his answer setting up his claims and praying for the relief required. A cross-bill cannot introduce new parties, or a new and independent controversy, but may be used for purposes of discovery or for the determination of any issue subordinate to that involved in the original bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-bill must relate to matters in original bill; cannot create an independent cause of action or new parties without leave. It must aver all facts essential to sustain the defendant's right and disclose the relation between the remedy sought and the principal suit. Leave of court and due notice usually required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-bill procedural consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: After the original bill is answered the plaintiff must answer the cross-bill, and until this is done the cause will not be heard. If the plaintiff withdraws the action after a cross-bill has been filed and served upon him, a decree pro confesso on the cross-bill may be taken by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a cross-bill imposes on plaintiff the duty to respond before hearing; withdrawal after service may expose plaintiff to decree against him on cross-bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental bill — when permissible and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any action in equity becomes defective after the filing of the original bill, whether by a change of the persons interested in the subject-matter of the suit, or by the occurrence of events enlarging or diminishing the rights of the parties, or whenever the plaintiff discovers facts essential to the proper decision of the controversy concerning which he had no information at the commencement of the action, he may file a supplemental bill alleging the new matter and thereby making it a part of his original claim. A supplemental bill must not vary the character of the suit or the cause of action; and can be filed only by leave of the court, for sufficient reasons and upon proper notice to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supplemental bills to add newly discovered parties, subsequent infringements, effects of patent extension, bankruptcy/assignee issues, etc. Must not change the character of suit; leave and notice required. Courts differ on reissue-pending-suit issues; can be waived by defendant's acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental bill for subsequent infringements and for patent extensions/reissues
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant has been guilty of additional infringements since the institution of the suit, these may be incorporated in the cause of action by a supplemental bill at any time before the plaintiff's evidence is closed. When the patent is extended during the litigation, and the infringement continues under the extension, a supplemental bill based on the extension may be filed, and the plaintiff can then recover for the entire injury in the single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental bills can cover infringements occurring after suit started and can incorporate extensions of patent term so damages for whole period can be recovered in one action. Filing on re-issue pending suit is contested — some cases require new bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental bill for rehearing/newly discovered evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When the plaintiff obtains a rehearing after the dismissal of his bill, upon the ground of newly discovered evidence, a supplemental bill is necessary, setting up the evidence and showing that it is material and could not have been produced by reasonable diligence on the former trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental bill must plead materiality and due diligence in failing to discover evidence earlier. Courts require allegations that evidence could not have been produced earlier with reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments to bill or answer — right before replication; leave after
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the filing of the replication amendments may be made, as a matter of right, in the bill or answer, but after replication no material alteration in either is allowed, except by leave of the court upon notice to the adverse party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend freely before replication. After replication, need court leave and notice; courts will deny leave if amendment could with reasonable diligence have been sooner introduced, changes character of pleading, or is offered for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for allowing amendments (examples of permissive grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority to permit amendments is conferred upon the court for the furtherance of justice, and to relieve the parties from the consequences of their unavoidable ignorance or mistake, and this authority may be exercised at any stage of the proceedings when its necessity becomes apparent. Thus where the evidence discloses that the description of the parties in the bill is incorrect, or that a different re-issue is in force from the one recited in the bill, or where the allegations of a bill brought by an assignee are broad enough to embrace, but do not specifically mention, claims for past infringements, or where the answer and the defendant's proof set up new matter in avoidance of his liability for the infringing acts, the plaintiff may amend the bill by the correction of the error, the enlargement of the insufficient allegation, or the insertion of new facts to meet the evidence and answer of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will allow amendments to cure mistakes disclosed by evidence (e.g., party description, re-issue number, add claims for past infringements, add missing prior user names) so pleadings conform to proof, unless other evidence shows plaintiff cannot be defeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on amendments (examples of denials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to amend will not be granted where the proposed amendment could with reasonable diligence have been sooner introduced, nor where it changes the character of the pleading, or is evidently offered for the purpose of delay. An amendment changing the character of the bill is not usually allowed after a hearing, or after the case is set down for a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court balances justice vs. prejudice/delay. Late amendments that introduce new defenses or fundamentally change causes are normally denied; motions to amend and for foreign commissions may be denied where proof shows amendment cannot be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of amendment on admissibility of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment of an answer under leave of court does not render evidence admissible which was properly objected to before the amendment; but evidence taken without objection in the presence of the adverse party may be received and considered under the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments do not retroactively cure prior admissibility rulings. However, unobjected-to evidence already taken may be used after amendment by agreement or when no surprise occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues of fact in equity patent cases — modes of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues of fact, in actions in equity for infringement, are always determined by the court, in accordance with its own views as to the significance and weight of the evidence presented. Various methods of investigating facts exist. The court may hear the testimony of the witnesses orally, or it may have evidence offered in the form of depositions. Feigned issues may be framed and sent to a jury in a court of law, or submitted to a special jury impanelled in the court of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity courts are the primary fact-finders; they may use oral testimony, depositions, feigned issues to a jury, or special juries depending on circumstances and discretion. Choice of mode depends on court's need for assistance and the nature of issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigned issues and jury trials — advisory nature and statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When facts are first passed upon by a jury ... the verdict is merely advisory, and may be departed from by the court. The act of 1875 enables [equity courts] to summon and impanel [a jury] consisting of not less than five nor more than twelve persons, to present to them such issues as it deems expedient, and to proceed upon their verdict in the same manner as if the issues had been tried at law. The submission of feigned issues to a jury is now a matter entirely within the discretion of the court, and no appeal will lie from its refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A jury's verdict in equity is generally advisory; statute allows empanelling juries of 5–12 and treating verdicts like law trials when the court chooses. Ordering a jury is discretionary; refusal is not appealable, though higher court may sometimes remand for jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret trial prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: That a secret trial of a patent suit cannot be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent suits must not be tried in secret; proceedings should follow openness requirements (Opinion Atty. Gen. cited).
